interest: This file provides valuable documentary evidence of how the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP) managed the delicate balance between acute domestic shortages, inflation, and international trade during the early Allied Occupation of Japan. It is particularly interesting for illustrating SCAP's economic philosophy regarding price controls: officials explicitly documented the catastrophic November 1945 experiment with decontrolling fish and vegetables, which caused runaway prices and forced the reinstatement of rationing in March 1946. Furthermore, the documents show how SCAP tied domestic compliance to international aid, warning Japanese fishermen and farmers that continuing imports of critical petroleum and fertilizer depended on their keeping perishable foodstuffs out of black markets.
overview: This file (894.5017, May 29, 1946 – June 23, 1948) documents economic controls, commodity pricing, and food distribution in occupied Japan. It opens with a May 1946 State Department communication to the British Embassy establishing an equitable export ceiling price and quality grade for Japanese stockpiles of antimony. The remainder of the file, spanning December 1947 to June 1948, centers on the enforcement of strict price caps and rationing schemes for perishable foodstuffs—primarily fish and vegetables—overseen by the Price Control and Rationing Division of SCAP's Economic and Scientific Section. Through diplomatic despatches, public press statements, and the formal issuance of SCAPIN 1910 under Directive No. 3, the file illustrates occupation efforts to curb rampant inflation, stamp out food black markets, and secure equitable food distribution among the Japanese public.

subfiles.about: Informs the British Embassy of the quality grade and agreed ceiling price for exportable Japanese antimony stockpiles.
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Acting Chief, Japanese and Korean Economic Division, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman of the State Department's Japanese and Korean Economic Division replies to a telephone inquiry from Douglass Campbell of the British Embassy regarding Japanese antimony stocks. Whitman cites a cable from the Supreme Commander confirming that the antimony grade is reported at 98.5 percent purity or higher. Following consultations among the State Department, the Civilian Production Administration, and the United States Commercial Company, an equitable price was set at 18.5 cents per pound delivered in New York City, or roughly 17.0 cents f.o.b. Japanese port.
subfiles.title: Letter from Roswell H. Whitman to Douglass Campbell regarding Japanese Antimony Stocks and Ceiling Price
subfiles.to: Douglass Campbell, Raw Materials Section, British Embassy, Washington, D. C.

subfiles.about: Transmits SCAP public statements on newly established price and distribution controls over perishable foods in Japan.
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan transmits Despatch No. 1467 to the Secretary of State, enclosing statements by SCAP Price Control and Rationing Division officials N. A. Stitt and H. F. Alber. The statements aimed to draw public attention to newly established price and rationing controls over perishable foods, particularly fish and vegetables, to ensure equitable food distribution. The despatch notes that full texts and summaries of these statements were widely published across major Japanese newspapers, including Mainichi, Nippon Keizai, Asahi, Yomiuri, Jiji Shimpo, and Tokyo Shimbun.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1467 from the Acting Political Adviser for Japan regarding Statements on Price Control and Rationing of Perishable Foods

subfiles.about: Publicizes a speech by SCAP official N. A. Stitt urging Tokyo fish and vegetable retailers to support price control enforcement.
subfiles.from: Public Information Office, General Headquarters, Far East Command
subfiles.summary: A press release issued by the GHQ Far East Command Public Information Office reports on an address given by N. A. Stitt of SCAP's Price Control and Rationing Division to fish and vegetable dealer representatives in Tokyo. Stitt emphasized that dealers occupy a crucial position between producers and consumers and are essential to the success of the government's enforcement campaign for perishable food controls. He observed that the Japanese government recognized that controlling staple rice alone was insufficient, and noted that regional conferences were underway with Eighth Army military government teams to ensure effective enforcement.
subfiles.title: SCAP Press Release: Statement by N. A. Stitt to Vegetable and Fish Dealers on Enforcement Campaign

subfiles.about: Articulates SCAP's policy rationale for maintaining strict price caps and rationing on fish and vegetables to combat black markets and inflation.
subfiles.from: H. F. Alber, Chief, Price Control & Rationing Division, Economic & Scientific Section, GHQ, SCAP
subfiles.summary: At a press conference in Tokyo, H. F. Alber, Chief of SCAP's Price Control and Rationing Division, explains why fish and vegetables must remain subject to strict price and distribution controls pursuant to SCAP Directive No. 3. He argues that decontrol would devastate wage earners and salaried families, citing the November 1945 decontrol fiasco that provoked astronomical price inflation and forced the reimposition of controls in March 1946. Alber further reminds farmers and fishermen that their industries depend heavily on imported petroleum and fertilizer provided by the Allies, making it their duty to channel supplies through official distribution channels rather than lucrative black markets.
subfiles.title: Press Conference Statement by H. F. Alber on Control of Fish and Vegetables
subfiles.to: Press conference attendees and general public

subfiles.about: Transmits SCAPIN 1910 confirming that fish and vegetables are classified as essential commodities in short supply subject to mandatory controls.
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan forwards Despatch No. 382 to the Department of State, enclosing SCAPIN 1910 dated June 15, 1948. The despatch explains that while fish and vegetables had been continuously rationed and sold at controlled prices under Directive No. 3 (SCAPIN 47) since September 1945, SCAPIN 1910 formally reaffirms in writing that these foods are essential commodities in short supply. The administrative action served to officially signal SCAP's insistence on the continued rationing and price regulation of perishable foodstuffs by the Japanese Government.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 382 from the Acting Political Adviser for Japan regarding Price and Distribution Controls Over Fish and Vegetables

subfiles.about: Formally directs the Japanese Government to maintain price and distribution controls over fish and vegetables under Directive No. 3.
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (by Colonel R. M. Levy, Adjutant General)
subfiles.summary: SCAPIN 1910, issued by GHQ SCAP to the Japanese Government, references Directive No. 3 (SCAPIN 47) of September 22, 1945, which required the Japanese authorities to maintain firm price and distribution controls on essential commodities in short supply. Citing persistent worldwide food shortages and the imperative to maximize indigenous foodstuffs, SCAP officially designates fish and vegetables as integral and indispensable components of the Japanese diet. Consequently, the memorandum explicitly places them within the purview of Directive No. 3, ordering continued strict controls over their pricing and distribution.
subfiles.title: SCAPIN 1910: Memorandum for the Japanese Government on Price and Distribution Controls Over Fish and Vegetables
